HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer to both parts of the question):

Amber reached its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE), and it peaked during the interval 3300–3000 BCE — equivalent to CE −3300 to −3000, or 5250–4950 calBP — where the amber Z-score plateaus at its series maximum of Z = +1.54 for four consecutive 100-year anchor points (3300, 3200, 3100 and 3000 BCE), coinciding with the "MN" (Middle Neolithic) period group in capital.csv. This peak plateau sits atop an already-elevated stage: amber held the second-highest value (Z = +1.46) throughout 4000–3400 BCE, so the 4th millennium BCE as a whole has a mean amber Z of +1.484 — by far the highest of any millennium in the record — after which amber collapses (Z ≤ +0.37 from 2900 BCE onward and mostly negative thereafter). Caveat on the boundary: the interpolated series holds the maximum value continuously across CE −3300 to −3000, and the plateau's final anchor year, 3000 BCE, sits exactly on the 4th/3rd-millennium boundary; under a naive floor-binning convention this creates a nominal tie in bin maxima, which is resolved decisively in favor of the 4th millennium BCE by bin means (+1.484 for the 4th millennium vs −0.148 for the 3rd, on raw anchors), consistent with the strict archaeological convention that the 4th millennium BCE spans 4000–3001 BCE. Note also that the interpolated ≥1.0 envelope extends back to CE −4018, but its early edge is a linear-interpolation artifact across the −1.07 → +1.46 step between 4100 and 4000 BCE and is not treated as the peak's start; the reported peak interval is anchored to the raw observations at 3300–3000 BCE.

This peak crowns an already-elevated 4th millennium (second-highest plateau Z = +1.46 during 4000–3400 BCE; millennium mean Z = +1.484, the highest of any millennium), after which amber values collapse (Z ≤ +0.37 from 2900 BCE, mostly negative thereafter). Boundary caveat: the plateau's final anchor year, 3000 BCE, lies exactly on the 4th/3rd-millennium boundary; naive floor-binning yields a nominal max tie, resolved in favor of the 4th millennium BCE by bin means (+1.484 vs −0.148) and by the strict convention 4th millennium BCE = 4000–3001 BCE. The interpolated ≥1.0 envelope's early edge (CE −4018) is a linear-interpolation artifact and was not used as the peak start.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded all three files, verifying chronology consistency: time_series_data.csv CE ascending 1-yr steps with calBP = 1950 − CE exactly; capital.csv BCE positive and descending at 100-yr steps (comma-decimal quoted parsing); pollen file descending with the same calBP convention. 2) Cross-validated capital.csv Zamber against raw Amber in time_series_data.csv via CE = −BCE: identical at all 37 overlapping anchors (max abs diff 0.0). 3) Treated the 37 raw 100-year Amber anchors as ground truth; Amber_inter (fully populated, step interpolation) used only to confirm plateau continuity. 4) Descriptive statistics of Amber, Amber_inter, Zamber. 5) Identified the maximum (Z = 1.54) and its contiguous anchor interval (3300–3000 BCE), converted to CE and calBP. 6) Ranked BCE millennia by bin max and bin mean under the strict 4th-millennium-BCE = 4000–3001 BCE convention; performed a floor-binning sensitivity check showing the 3000-BCE boundary tie is resolved by bin means. 7) Documented the interpolated ≥1.0 envelope as context with an explicit interpolation-artifact caveat.
